Chapter 3: When Algorithms Decide Who Gets a Second Chance
Picture this: in the hushed halls of the justice system, there’s a new kind of decision-maker quietly at work—an algorithm that’s supposed to predict whether someone will reoffend. Judges, often overwhelmed with packed courtrooms and incomplete information, are turning to these risk assessment tools for guidance. They’re built from mountains of data—past arrests, old convictions—and they boil each person down to a single score. That number? It can decide everything, from how high bail is set to the length of a prison sentence.
Imagine standing in front of a judge, waiting for your fate. Now, think about how it feels knowing that a computer-generated score could spell the difference between walking free and being locked up. These tools promise to strip away human bias and bring some consistency to a system that’s struggled with fairness. But here’s something to consider: instead of erasing old disparities, these models often copy and magnify them.
Take the case of a young man arrested for something minor. The algorithm, trained on patterns from neighborhoods with heavy police patrols, flags his home address as a red flag. The judge, trusting the computer, sets his bail way too high—so he can’t go home. And then, the spiral begins: he misses work, money runs out, and stress just piles on.
The issue isn’t just that these models sometimes get it wrong. It’s deeper than that—they tend to reinforce themselves. Cops are sent over and over to places with lots of arrests, which means more people get picked up, feeding even more data into the model. The algorithm isn’t breaking the cycle; it’s making it stronger.
Most folks caught up in this system have no clue how their risk score was calculated. The formulas are secret—guarded by the companies selling them to courts and police. Even if someone suspects the computer got it wrong, there’s almost nothing they can do to fight it. The logic stays hidden, locked behind lines of code.
And the fallout? It spreads far beyond the courtroom. Families are split apart. Neighborhoods feel less stable. Bit by bit, trust in the justice system fades. What started as a promise of fairness turns into a reality where the most vulnerable get trapped by rules they can’t even see.
And it’s not just happening in courtrooms. Police departments use similar models to guess where crimes might happen next. Officers are sent, again and again, to certain neighborhoods—often communities of color—because that’s what the software predicts. Residents end up feeling constantly watched, and crime rates? They don’t really budge.
So, what’s the real lesson here? Algorithms, if we let them run unchecked, can lock in the very inequalities we want to fix. They might look objective, but their choices come straight from the data they’re built on—and from the people who design them.
For people inside this system, it’s frustrating and often feels hopeless. A mother might wonder why her son was denied bail. A whole community may ask why their streets are always under watchful eyes. But the answers, if they exist, are buried deep in algorithms that almost no one understands.
The solution isn’t to throw out every data-driven tool. Instead, we need to insist on accountability. These models should be transparent—their workings open for everyone to see. There has to be a way to challenge mistakes and fix them. Only then can we make sure algorithms actually serve justice, instead of standing in its way.
